faq.question: How do I calculate electricity units from watts?
faq.answer: Multiply the appliance's power in watts by the hours it runs, then divide by 1,000. A 1,500-watt appliance running for 2 hours uses 1,500 × 2 ÷ 1,000 = 3 units (kWh). Add up all your appliances over the billing period to get your total units.

faq.question: How much electricity does a 1.5-ton AC use?
faq.answer: It depends on the model, its star rating and the outside temperature. As a rough guide, an inverter AC averaging about 900 watts while running uses around 3.6 units in a 4-hour night, or about 108 units a month. Check the AC's BEE label for its rated yearly consumption, or measure it with your meter.

faq.question: Who gets 200 free units of electricity in Tamil Nadu?
faq.answer: Domestic consumers who use 500 units or less in a two-month billing cycle, from 10 May 2026. If you use more than 500 units, you stay on the earlier structure with 100 free units and higher charges on the next 100 units.

faq.question: Why did my TNEB bill jump when I used only a few more units?
faq.answer: If you crossed 500 units in the two-month cycle, you lost the extra 100 free units and moved to the higher slab structure. At 500 units the bill is ₹1,570; at 501 units it's ₹2,048.40, a jump of ₹478.40.

faq.question: Does switching appliances off at the plug save electricity?
faq.answer: Yes, a little. Devices on standby draw a few watts each, all day. A router, set-top box and chargers drawing 30 watts between them use about 43 units over two months. Switching off what you don't need overnight trims that, though the AC and water heater matter far more.
